title: Randomized competitive ratio of list update
formal: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio of online list update against an oblivious adversary in the full-cost model: \[\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}=\inf\{r\in[1,\infty):r\text{ is achievable under the definition below}\}.\] Give its value to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The same competitive factor must work for lists of every finite size, with an additive constant allowed to depend on the size and initial order. No predictions or advice about future requests are supplied.
definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the item set is \([n]\) and an initial list \(L_0\) is a permutation of these items. A request sequence \(\sigma=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\in[n]^T\) has arbitrary finite length \(T\ge0\), is fixed independently of all online randomness, and is revealed one request at a time. The online rule must finish serving \(x_t\) before learning \(x_{t+1}\); it is not told the remaining sequence or its length. Accessing an item in current position \(j\), counting from one, costs \(j\). After this access, that item may be moved any distance toward the front at zero cost. Each other exchange of adjacent items costs one. Paid exchanges may be performed between accesses, including before serving a revealed request, and every such exchange is charged. The free move changes only the accessed item’s position and preserves the relative order of all other items. Items are never inserted or deleted. The total cost is the sum of access costs and paid exchanges. The offline optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)\) is the minimum cost of a legal schedule starting from the same \(L_0\), with advance knowledge of all of \(\sigma\), under exactly these access and exchange rules. A randomized online rule chooses each finite legal service action using only the revealed request prefix, its previous actions and its private random state. Abstract probability distributions over actions are permitted, with no bound on computational work or memory; all expectations must be well defined. Each request is served with finitely many exchanges on each realization. A real \(r\ge1\) is achievable if \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall L_0\ \exists A_{n,L_0,r}\ \exists\beta_{n,L_0,r}\in[0,\infty)\ \forall T\ge0\ \forall\sigma\in[n]^T:\quad \mathbb E[\mathrm{cost}_{A_{n,L_0,r}}(\sigma)]\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)+\beta_{n,L_0,r}.\] The rule and finite additive constant are chosen before the future requests, so neither may depend on \(\sigma\) or \(T\). Expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness alone. The infimum is over such common factors \(r\); it need not be attained. This is the full-cost convention \(j\), not the partial-cost convention \(j-1\). All costs and the ratio are dimensionless.
why: List update is a basic model of a data structure adapting to changing demand without knowing future accesses. Its optimal randomized ratio would quantify the value of randomization in a simple online problem whose deterministic analogue is well understood. The unresolved constant gap makes it a precise long-standing benchmark in competitive analysis.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 primary source states the classical randomized bounds \(1.5\le\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}\le1.6\) and defines access cost by the position counted from one. This interval has width \(0.1\), so it does not certify the required absolute error \(0.01\).

The same paper investigates algorithms assisted by predictions. Their guarantees involve additional information unavailable in the ordinary online problem specified here; those results do not settle the classical optimal ratio.

A related lower bound of \(1.50084\), proved by Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel, is explicitly for the partial-cost model, where the first item costs zero to access. Changing the charge by one on every request can change a competitive ratio, so that theorem is not asserted here as a stronger full-cost lower bound.

The additive constant is independent of the entire request sequence and its length. It permits a fixed initial-order cost but cannot absorb a cost that grows with the number of requests. The infimum formulation also permits a limiting optimal ratio without assuming that a best online rule exists.

progress.text: The 2025 source attributes the randomized upper bound 1.6 to Albers, von Stengel and Werchner.
Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel publish a lower bound of 1.50084 for the distinct partial-cost model; the checked author manuscript is dated 21 June 1999.
List Update with Prediction records the classical 1.5–1.6 gap while proving guarantees for algorithms supplied with predictions.

answer_criterion: Provide an unambiguously specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}|\le1/100\). Certified upper and lower bounds that imply this error are sufficient, even if no algorithm attains the infimum. The proof must use full access costs, an oblivious adversary, all list sizes and sequence lengths, and the permitted additive constant. Bounds for a restricted family of online rules, for a fixed bounded list size, for algorithms given predictions or for the partial-cost convention do not by themselves certify the requested value.
status_note: The April 2025 source records the unresolved full-cost randomized 1.5–1.6 gap. The checked 1.50084 theorem concerns partial costs and is not used as a stronger bound for this card. A bounded later-work search through 2026-09-15 found no result certifying the specified optimal constant to absolute error 1/100; no exhaustive current-status claim is made.

importance.reason: Even for an elementary self-organizing list, the optimal benefit of randomization in competitive performance is unknown.

category_assignment.reason: Measures competitive ratio against offline OPT under online requests, rather than RAM running time.

sentences: An online list serves each request before seeing the next, and access costs the item’s position counted from one.
The accessed item may move forward for free, while other adjacent exchanges cost one.
Randomized performance is compared with an optimal offline schedule under the same rules and initial order.
The checked full-cost bounds leave the optimal competitive factor between 1.5 and 1.6.
The benchmark asks for a Lean-certified approximation of this factor to absolute error at most one hundredth.
